title: Model integration, evaluation, and monitoring boundaries
sources: Python documentation: data validation, logging, and packaging concepts
scikit-learn documentation concepts: train/test separation, metrics, and model persistence caveats
masterChecklist: AI/ML integration: data preparation, model-service API boundaries, evaluation and monitoring concepts
Data engineering: CSV/JSON, SQL, pandas/NumPy basics, data quality, pipelines
Monitoring, metrics, tracing, alerting, on-call basics, incident-friendly logging
whyItMatters: A model that produces a number in a notebook is not automatically safe or useful in an application. Production use needs clear input/output contracts, evaluation evidence, versioned data/model context, monitored behavior, and a safe fallback when the result is missing or unreliable.
simpleExplanation: Model integration is a boundary: prepare validated features, call a model through a small interface, validate the output, and decide what the product does with it. Evaluation checks a model against labelled/known data before release. Monitoring checks whether inputs, outputs, errors, and user-impact signals change after release.
mentalModel: A model is one specialist inside a clinic, not the whole clinic. The receptionist checks the form, the specialist gives an opinion with limits, and the clinic records outcomes to see whether the service remains safe and useful.
outcomes: Separate feature preparation, prediction, and product decision responsibilities.
Define a small model input/output contract.
Recognize train/test leakage and why held-out evaluation matters.
Record model/data/version context with safe metrics.
Design a fallback or review path rather than blindly trusting every score.

realWorldExample.scenario: A study app uses a model score to suggest a next lesson.
realWorldExample.riskWithoutSetup: The app sends unvalidated values to a changing model, treats a score as certain, stores private raw inputs in logs, and has no way to notice that new learner behavior differs from the evaluation data.
realWorldExample.professionalApproach: Validate feature shape/range, version the model and feature rule, evaluate on held-out representative data, log safe aggregate/error signals, set confidence/eligibility rules, and fall back to a transparent rules-based suggestion when the model is unavailable or outside its intended scope.

explanation: Feature preparation validates the actual product inputs before any scoring decision.
The score/suggestion boundary is deliberately separate so it can later be replaced by a versioned model adapter.
The deterministic function is not an ML model; it lets learners test the surrounding contract without downloading or trusting an opaque artifact.
A real evaluation would compare predictions against labelled outcomes using an appropriate metric and held-out data, not the same data used to train/tune the model.
Monitoring should report safe aggregate quality/latency/error signals and investigate distribution changes without logging unnecessary private raw data.
workedExample.expectedOutput: review foundations because 3/10 is below the simple threshold.
workedExample.safeExperiment: Try invalid counts and see the boundary reject them. Then change the threshold and explain why a threshold decision needs evaluation evidence and product review.

procedure: Define the product decision and a non-model fallback before selecting an algorithm.
Document supported features, units, allowed ranges, missing-value policy, and data-minimization rules.
Separate training/evaluation data from deployment input; prevent labels/future information from leaking into features.
Evaluate on held-out representative data with a metric that matches the product cost of errors.
Version the model, feature transformation, evaluation dataset identity, and threshold/policy together.
Validate incoming features and outgoing predictions at the service boundary.
Monitor safe aggregate inputs/outputs, latency, errors, and outcome signals; define review/retrain/rollback triggers.

commonMistakes.mistake: Evaluating on the same data used to train or tune a model.
commonMistakes.why: The result can look strong while failing on new users or future data.
commonMistakes.avoid: Use held-out evaluation and a clear split policy.

commonMistakes.mistake: Logging full raw learner features to debug predictions.
commonMistakes.why: It can create unnecessary privacy and retention risk.
commonMistakes.avoid: Log minimal safe identifiers/aggregates and use controlled investigation paths.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating a numerical score as a final decision with no fallback or review path.
commonMistakes.why: Models can be unavailable, out of scope, or wrong in costly ways.
commonMistakes.avoid: Set eligibility/confidence/product rules and retain a transparent fallback.

guidedSteps: Validate type and range before division.
Define what zero available lessons means for this small exercise.
Return a named feature dictionary rather than a positional mystery value.
Use a transparent threshold decision as a stand-in boundary.
Name one evaluation/monitoring fact required before replacing it with a model.
checks: States that a deterministic demo is not model evaluation.
hints: Use type(value) is int: bool is an int subclass but not a meaningful count.
Reject negative done and zero available before dividing.
Keep the decision rule separate from feature preparation.
lab.solutionExplanation: The lab practices the reliable code around a model boundary: validated inputs, named features, and a clear product decision. It intentionally does not claim to train or evaluate ML; those require representative data, a defined metric, and versioned evaluation evidence.
challenges: Predict the risk of using future completion data as an input to recommend the next lesson.
Find the privacy bug: logging the full learner profile for every score.
Experiment: add a fallback when the feature is outside the supported range.

projectConnection.milestone: Implement a validated feature/preference boundary with a transparent fallback. Draft the held-out evaluation metric, safe monitoring signals, and rollback rule required before any model replaces the local rule.
projectConnection.definitionOfDone: The project validates input/output contracts, distinguishes deterministic demo logic from evaluated ML, documents feature/model/version context, and provides a safe fallback/review path.

assessment.question: Why use held-out data for model evaluation?
assessment.answer: It gives evidence about performance on data not used to fit or tune the model.
assessment.explanation: Training-data scores can overstate real-world performance.

assessment.question: What should a model-service boundary validate?
assessment.answer: Supported input shape/range and usable output shape before product logic relies on them.
assessment.explanation: Annotations or a model call alone do not guarantee valid runtime data.

assessment.question: Why keep a fallback path?
assessment.answer: A model can fail, be unavailable, or be outside its intended scope; the product still needs a safe behavior.
assessment.explanation: Fallbacks make the system more resilient and transparent.
